phrases.english_text: Just right over in the other hollow—Cloud Hollow. Where the church is, up that hollow. Down that way, I was born. We moved around in that area when I was growing up. The last time we moved it was straight from where the church is at the end of the hollow is. Still there—that is where we lived. And when we moved from there “Let's move for good from here,” our dad said. “We are going to travel.” We came across. Grandfather lived across by the hollow little ridge. We came there. And then, “We are moving from this hollow”, he told him. “Why? You all have been living around here a long time.” he said. “That is true. It has to be. I am going to get closer to my work.” And then we came up through the hollow. Dropping things. We came over. Then we went back into another hollow. And, where we came out, there was a little house, close. It was just this wide [gestures]. “We can live there until the summer,” he said. And water and food—there is a creek. “You all can fish there or catch crawdads. And in the evening we will eat good.” We would go there. Norman would follow us all the time. Second— in the family we were half brothers, that one. My dad was his dad, that one. His mom lived nearby. But they moved when we got there. So he stayed with us. He would be with us when we would go to the water. We would go catch lots of fish. We would eat fast, in the evening. He had a sawmill, that boss. My dad worked there. And we would go to the water every day. And then, about two years we lived there, their sawmill broke down. “I guess that’s all for us,” they said. “I guess we will go back, then.” ‘Loaded up and came back up the hollow. We came back down, close to Grandfather’s house. We came back again. [Grandfather said] “That house is still there—where you all lived.” “We are headed back to it,” he said. So, we went back over there. Then they said “Let's make a church on the hill.” They said, “There, before Anigvluyo.” It was flat. And that was our church. We would walk that far. And went there on Sunday or Saturday. At night we would be coming back. And come back there [to the original house]. It was closer for us to go, when we moved there. Then they talked about making a church right there on the hill. “On the ridge,” they said. Then they started cutting wood up, the adults. And was dragging limbs around, clearing for the workers. We made it. My dad’s brother had a sawmill there. He started milling. He milled all that, where that little building is. We made a church there. We went in there. Jen was an old lady then, she would walk using her cane. She would come up. It was like this, there. She would come in on Sunday morning.

phrases.english_text: “I really think she was older than that,” I told my brother. “From what I heard, she was 114, they say,” he told me. There is a young man that lives right there. We talked the other day. “Have you seen that old lady they talk about?” he said to me. “Who, Jenny?” I said that. “How old she was ?” he told me. Then I went to Jay ‘couple days, and looked. Me and that young man that lives right there. He said: ”’Jenny Birdchopper--’ was written,” he said, “’--birthday 144 years old.’” “I believe it,” I told him. “I think it is true,” I told him. When she died, I was over there, we were talking. She had some flowers planted—just right there. She was fixing and cleaning them. ‘ She w at them. “I guess you all can do it now,” she told them. “But for now I am going in the house and rest,” she told them. I thought she was saying ‘just for now.’ “I am going to rest for now. You all stand here.” She went into the house. I was standing there, looking at them [the flowers]. And then my playmate came. “What are you looking at?” He said. “Jen was talking to those flowers she has planted there,” I told him. “All the time. Every day.” “But I am going into the house and rest,” she told them. I said to him, “She must have got tired.” “Let's go over to the water. There is two buckets, over there, we will get,” he told me. I said, “OK, five gallons.” “Five gallons full,” he had, setting. We got them and brought them up. And we set them there. The one they call Lol was cooking there. Ones name was Nvtsi. And then she said “You all eat. You all wake up Jen, we will eat,” or “You go give her something to eat. She has been working outside.” They could not wake her up. Her head was doing this [gestures]. They were doing this—they raised her arm—it would just hang down. They were rubbing her. “Jen is gone,” they said. “She is not doing anything. Lay her in the other bed.” When we did this, she went everywhere. She did not have any bones in her at all. When you did this [gestures] it bent all over and would raise and flop like this. They just rolled her up and got her and put her there. Laid her there just like laying a quilt down. That is how they did it. They laid her.

phrases.english_text: Diganiyisgi Sigil, but Sigil lived towards Colorado. Another one lives in Kansas City, Wili. And ᎠᏓᏬᏍᎩ How do they say Oregon? He still lives there. I guess he is wealthy now. phrases.english_text: Diganiyisgi Sigil, but Sigil lived towards Colorado. Another one lives in Kansas City, Wili. And ᎠᏓᏬᏍᎩ How do they say Oregon? He still lives there. I guess he is wealthy now. He was a wood cutter. And, another one, Tom. That was his sibling. Tom was his name, that lived there. Gvnenulisgi was a son in-law, there. Married to Kehogi. He lived there, too. It's just like the same thing happened to him, too—he just got old. I don’t know how old that one was. He was older, too. And the rest of them, we are about the same age, we brought them up. Our dads, our grandmas, I mean [raised them]. Our mom, too. She was good. But then Dad left there. Just our mom was around there. But she was a singing woman, we would laugh at her too. Mel used to laugh at her. That’s the way it was—how we came.

phrases.english_text: Yeah, and if you go up the hollow, it's like this—it comes out way on top. It comes, then it comes back this way. And that’s how he came. There is a crossroad, over there. Where it goes up a wide road. It’s a ridge—there is a crossroad. He came across there. And, over there, on the hill, it's like this. And it comes down, this way, where that building is—beside. It comes out, just on the other side. It goes that way. He came across. Then, he went across the water and went back into the hollow. He would go a little way and went back up. He went, through the cave, for that long it was level, when he got there. He would cross the water and get to the church.

Mel was little, just little, about yea tall [gestures]. ‘Just now walking good, or she was walking good. The other was bigger. Corene, me, and Arch were adults. We were sitting there. And dad used to hunt all the time. At night time he would be listening, to the dogs he had, that chased coyotes and foxes. He would be listening—Arch and him. They were sitting there, it was dark. “I am going to the woods tonight,” I told him. “Are you going to look for possums?” “I might bring some when I am coming back,” I told him. “OK, watch yourself.” “OK, I will be carrying a light.” I told him. “Ok. ‘Dogs are tied up right there. Take them. They are old, they will not take you very far away.” He told me. I kept walking and came on up. I was walking on a ridge over there. About halfway, where I said, there was a crossroad. About there, I stopped, and the dogs scattered out. They barked way over there. So, I thought “I will just sit right here, at this tree.” There were some places to sit, so I sat down. I was sitting there, listening. When they came up they went that way. They got quite far that way. They might have found a coyote, I thought. I am going to get closer, I thought. And I got up, and I started walking. Somewhere on top I stopped, and I sat down. I was sitting there and the light started getting low. I ran out of coal oil. It got dark. “I guess I am just going to sit here. I have a fire,” I thought. “I am just going to sit here.” They were chasing just over there. They went by, and came back. I said “Did you all catch it?” They just laid down. I was really getting suspicious. It was dark now. We had never been that far. Where I was, there was a good road. I thought “What am I going to do now?” There was a lightning bug flying right there, I caught it. It was shining good light when I held it, and I took its tail off. I stuck it on [my clothes] and then another—they started coming out. I was catching them, putting them on my clothes, and then it was kind of light. Then I started walking. I followed the road. It was clear, right there—they were not going dim. It was good light. That was the way it was. I went off and got back to the house. “I really appreciate you, my God,” I told Him.

Mel was little, just little, about yea tall [gestures]. ‘Just now walking good, or she was walking good. The other was bigger. Corene, me, and Arch were adults. We were sitting there. And dad used to hunt all the time. At night time he would be listening, to the dogs he had, that chased coyotes and foxes. He would be listening—Arch and him. They were sitting there, it was dark. “I am going to the woods tonight,” I told him. “Are you going to look for possums?” “I might bring some when I am coming back,” I told him. “OK, watch yourself.” “OK, I will be carrying a light.” I told him. “Ok. ‘Dogs are tied up right there. Take them. They are old, they will not take you very far away.” He told me. I kept walking and came on up. I was walking on a ridge over there. About halfway, where I said, there was a crossroad. About there, I stopped, and the dogs scattered out. They barked way over there. So, I thought “I will just sit right here, at this tree.” There were some places to sit, so I sat down. I was sitting there, listening. When they came up they went that way. They got quite far that way. They might have found a coyote, I thought. I am going to get closer, I thought. And I got up, and I started walking. Somewhere on top I stopped, and I sat down. I was sitting there and the light started getting low. I ran out of coal oil. It got dark. “I guess I am just going to sit here. I have a fire,” I thought. “I am just going to sit here.” They were chasing just over there. They went by, and came back. I said “Did you all catch it?” They just laid down. I was really getting suspicious. It was dark now. We had never been that far. Where I was, there was a good road. I thought “What am I going to do now?” There was a lightning bug flying right there, I caught it. It was shining good light when I held it, and I took its tail off. I stuck it on [my clothes] and then another—they started coming out. I was catching them, putting them on my clothes, and then it was kind of light. Then I started walking. I followed the road. It was clear, right there—they were not going dim. It was good light. That was the way it was. I went off and got back to the house. “I really appreciate you, my God,” I told Him.

phrases.english_text: One time, this is myself—over there, where we lived. That good house, it was a ranch. We lived there. Mel was little, just little, about yea tall [gestures]. ‘Just now walking good, or she was walking good. The other was bigger. Corene, me, and Arch were adults. We were sitting there. And dad used to hunt all the time. At night time he would be listening, to the dogs he had, that chased coyotes and foxes. He would be listening—Arch and him. They were sitting there, it was dark. “I am going to the woods tonight,” I told him. “Are you going to look for possums?” “I might bring some when I am coming back,” I told him. “OK, watch yourself.” “OK, I will be carrying a light.” I told him. “Ok. ‘Dogs are tied up right there. Take them. They are old, they will not take you very far away.” He told me. I kept walking and came on up. I was walking on a ridge over there. About halfway, where I said, there was a crossroad. About there, I stopped, and the dogs scattered out. They barked way over there. So, I thought “I will just sit right here, at this tree.” There were some places to sit, so I sat down. I was sitting there, listening. When they came up they went that way. They got quite far that way. They might have found a coyote, I thought. I am going to get closer, I thought. And I got up, and I started walking. Somewhere on top I stopped, and I sat down. I was sitting there and the light started getting low. I ran out of coal oil. It got dark. “I guess I am just going to sit here. I have a fire,” I thought. “I am just going to sit here.” They were chasing just over there. They went by, and came back. I said “Did you all catch it?” They just laid down. I was really getting suspicious. It was dark now. We had never been that far. Where I was, there was a good road. I thought “What am I going to do now?” There was a lightning bug flying right there, I caught it. It was shining good light when I held it, and I took its tail off. I stuck it on [my clothes] and then another—they started coming out. I was catching them, putting them on my clothes, and then it was kind of light. Then I started walking. I followed the road. It was clear, right there—they were not going dim. It was good light. That was the way it was. I went off and got back to the house. “I really appreciate you, my God,” I told Him.

phrases.english_text: He gave me those to see, to go home with. “I really appreciate you. my God,” I told Him. “I would not have seen anything to think about, if it was not for you,” I told Him. He revealed that to me. The old man was sitting there when I came in. “Are you already back? I was going to go that way, in a little bit,” he said. He was concerned for me. I was doing good. “We went way over there, to the end.” I told him. “They were really chasing. They would go this way,” I told him. ”And then that way.” “Oh, I didn’t hear them,” he said. “I was thinking I better go look for them.” When we got back, I told them I was thankful we had a good time. “I will feed you tomorrow.” I told them. We went to sleep. And then—toward the last—I was going everywhere in the creek. Gigging crawdads [with a small gig spear]. That was it—nothing, nowhere else. Sometimes we made fence posts. Arch would be standing somewhere, sharpening them. And, when he would sharpen them, we would sell them and buy food. We would eat good in the evening. That is what we did all day. Or something. Or the old man would carve railroad ties. If we cut one somewhere, it would be laying there. He would carve it, when he got time. Then he would walk somewhere else, and carve another one. And when he would carve all of them, I would take a horse. I would hook them on, ‘gather them together, and take them up to where a truck would go. We would load them up. We would get them out of the hollow—we would haul them up. Arch would be going around carving posts somewhere. We were doing good. We would kill a hog. Dad would fatten them up, and then we would have food. Just flour, potatoes, and beans—we would buy that. And then we would be eating good. We were not starving. Now’days it is different.

phrases.syllabary_text: ᏙᏳᏗ ᏍᏈᏍᏛᏅ ᏙᎩᏃᎩᏌ Coffeyville ᎢᎾᏴ ᏥᎤᏬᎨᏙᎸ ᏌᏭ ᏳᏩᎦᏓ

phrases.english_text: We really sang at a lot of places. We went all the way to Coffeyville one time. We went and sang, and sang, with Danile. He enjoyed it. He drove us to Coffeyville. We found, where we were going, there was a lot of people. They were having a pie supper event. There were lots of people. They started buying them [pies]. When we left we filled us up with sweets. When we got back “What did you go do?” my mom said. “I went and sang,” I said to her. “You did something else. Your face is all strange,” she said. It was those sweets sticking to me—they put them everywhere in that car. We were just driving a little car. It was giving me a bath! We did not hardly bring any to eat. We smashed them, mostly. We were dropping them. It was good. We had a good trip. We went and sang. And Coren was about yea tall [gestures]. She was a singer we had with us, every now ‘then. She would say, “Are you going to help me sing? What am I going to sing? You are going to sing small. How am I going to sing small, I have a big voice?” “I don’t mean that.” He told her. He meant—you are going to sing alto.

phrases.english_text: That I was telling [before]—we went to the woods, and back and forth. We would carry two, and cut them down, and chop them up. We measured, and Arch would be walking behind us—sharp hammer on one side. And, what do they call them, wedges? That he would stick in, to split [the wood]. And, when they would kind of open up, then he would use a big axe to split. It would do this. He did it easy. He was experienced. And if the wood was this big [gestures] he would make one, then another, then another. He would make four or five good ones, ‘same size. He would sharpen them. When he sharpened them he would stand them up real quick. And that broad axe, it was kind of small, one side was sharp—he used one like that. He would peel the bark of one side, then the other. Then he would turn it around and then comb it a little, there. He would finish real quick. Yeah, he was experienced—Arch.
